title: Rehearsal First, Revision Second: Why Building Knowledge Comes Before Testing It [FREE RESOURCE]
author: Jamie Lee Clark
summary: Clark argues that retrieval practice is often used too early because teachers skip rehearsal, the stage in which new knowledge is actively connected to prior understanding, verbalised and stabilised. Drawing on Efrat Furst's model of how knowledge develops, he distinguishes rehearsal as construction of knowledge from retrieval practice as consolidation of what already exists. He lists what rehearsal is and is not, for instance pair talk and choral response for everyone rather than one student answering while others watch. He supports the case with a 2026 study of fourth-graders in which retrieval practice boosted recall of spelling rules but did nothing for application, and with Rosenshine's principle on practice and review. His rule of thumb is that if only some students have rehearsed an idea, none are ready for retrieval. The piece ends with promotion of a free template and paid resources, but the instructional argument is clear.
points: What looks like forgetting is often knowledge that was never properly constructed in the first place.
Rehearsal builds knowledge and retrieval practice maintains it, so confusing the two leads to quizzing students on hazy understanding.
Rehearsal must involve every student through pair talk, choral response or mini-whiteboards, not a single student answering for the class.
The 2026 spelling-rule study shows strong recall can coexist with weak application unless rehearsal occurs in meaningful contexts.
Worked examples and sentence starters let students rehearse with support before independent practice.
quotes: Rehearsal constructs the knowledge. It is the phase where new knowledge is actively formed, connected to prior understanding, verbalised, and stabilised before students are expected to retrieve it independently.

Students are frequently asked to retrieve knowledge through quizzes, starters, and recall activities when they never had sufficient time to rehearse it in the first place. The result is predictable: hazy answers, unstable understanding, and students who appear to “know it” during the lesson but cannot recall or apply it independently later.

The problem is often diagnosed as forgetting. In reality, the knowledge may never have been properly constructed in the first place. Rehearsal is the stage where new knowledge is actively processed, connected, verbalised, and stabilised before students are expected to retrieve it later.
The retrieval group recalled the rules far more accurately after one week. Then came the application task: actually using the rules correctly in sentences. Both groups performed almost identically.

Why? Because remembering a rule is not the same as being able to use it. Retrieval practice strengthened explicit recall — but fluent application requires something more: sufficient rehearsal in meaningful contexts, with the rule actually being used, not just retrieved.

Students need to practice and review in order to learn new facts and skills and in order to consolidate new learning. The review of previous learning can strengthen the connections among the material that students have learned.

A useful rule of thumb: if only some students have rehearsed the idea, none of them are ready for retrieval practice. Every student needs to have done the mental work before the quiz, the starter activity, or the spaced recall task will do its job.
